claim: ICEBs1 is an integrative and conjugative element of Bacillus subtilis.
source: We describe a benefit that ICEBs1, an integrative and conjugative element of Bacillus subtilis, provides to its host cells.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a defining characteristic of ICEBs1.

claim: Activation of ICEBs1 conferred a frequency-dependent selective advantage to host cells during biofilm formation.
source: Activation of ICEBs1 conferred a frequency-dependent selective advantage to host cells during two different developmental processes: biofilm formation and sporulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Activation of ICEBs1 conferred a frequency-dependent selective advantage to host cells during sporulation.
source: Activation of ICEBs1 conferred a frequency-dependent selective advantage to host cells during two different developmental processes: biofilm formation and sporulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The benefits of ICEBs1 were due to inhibition of biofilm-associated gene expression by ICEBs1-containing cells.
source: These benefits were due to inhibition of biofilm-associated gene expression and delayed sporulation by ICEBs1-containing cells, enabling them to exploit their neighbors and grow more prior to development.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by gene expression data in the manuscript.

claim: The benefits of ICEBs1 were due to delayed sporulation by ICEBs1-containing cells.
source: These benefits were due to inhibition of biofilm-associated gene expression and delayed sporulation by ICEBs1-containing cells, enabling them to exploit their neighbors and grow more prior to development.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by sporulation timing data in the manuscript.

claim: ICEBs1-containing cells exploit their neighbors and grow more prior to development.
source: These benefits were due to inhibition of biofilm-associated gene expression and delayed sporulation by ICEBs1-containing cells, enabling them to exploit their neighbors and grow more prior to development.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an interpretation of the fitness advantage data.

claim: devI (formerly ydcO) is necessary for inhibition of development by ICEBs1.
source: A single ICEBs1 gene, devI (formerly ydcO), was both necessary and sufficient for inhibition of development.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by deletion mutant data in the manuscript.

claim: devI (formerly ydcO) is sufficient for inhibition of development by ICEBs1.
source: A single ICEBs1 gene, devI (formerly ydcO), was both necessary and sufficient for inhibition of development.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ectopic expression data in the manuscript.

claim: Manipulation of host developmental programs allows ICEBs1 to increase host fitness.
source: Manipulation of host developmental programs allows ICEBs1 to increase host fitness, thereby increasing propagation of the element.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: Increasing host fitness increases propagation of ICEBs1.
source: Manipulation of host developmental programs allows ICEBs1 to increase host fitness, thereby increasing propagation of the element.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a logical consequence of increased host fitness.

claim: Conjugative elements and phages are abundant mobile genetic elements in bacteria.
source: Conjugative elements and phages are abundant mobile genetic elements in bacteria, capable of transferring DNA between cells (Frost et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Conjugative elements and phages are capable of transferring DNA between cells.
source: Conjugative elements and phages are abundant mobile genetic elements in bacteria, capable of transferring DNA between cells (Frost et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Integrative and conjugative elements (ICEs) appear to be the most widespread type of conjugative element.
source: Integrative and conjugative elements (ICEs) appear to be the most widespread type of conjugative element (Guglielmini et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: ICEs are found integrated in a host genome.
source: ICEs are found integrated in a host genome.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a defining characteristic of ICEs.

claim: When activated, ICEs excise and produce conjugation machinery that transfers the element DNA from the host cell to recipients.
source: When activated, they excise and produce conjugation machinery that transfers the element DNA from the host cell to recipients (Carraro and Burrus, 2015; Johnson and Grossman, 2015; Wozniak and Waldor, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: ICEs often carry 'cargo' genes that are not necessary for transfer but confer a phenotype to host cells.
source: ICEs often carry 'cargo' genes that are not necessary for transfer but confer a phenotype to host cells.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a known characteristic of ICEs.

claim: ICEs (conjugative transposons) were first identified because of the phenotypes conferred by cargo genes.
source: In fact, ICEs (conjugative transposons) were first identified because of the phenotypes conferred by cargo genes (Franke and Clewell, 1981).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Cargo genes include those encoding antibiotic resistances, metabolic pathways, and determinants of pathogenesis and symbiosis.
source: Cargo genes include those encoding antibiotic resistances, metabolic pathways, and determinants of pathogenesis and symbiosis (Johnson and Grossman, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Transfer of mobile elements between cells contributes to rapid evolution and spread of associated cargo genes and phenotypes.
source: Transfer of mobile elements between cells contributes to rapid evolution and spread of associated cargo genes and phenotypes (Frost et al., 2005; Treangen and Rocha, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The maintenance and transfer of mobile genetic elements requires host cellular resources.
source: Despite the benefits cargo genes can provide, the maintenance and transfer of mobile genetic elements requires host cellular resources and in some cases is lethal (Baltrus, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: In some cases, maintenance and transfer of mobile genetic elements is lethal.
source: Despite the benefits cargo genes can provide, the maintenance and transfer of mobile genetic elements requires host cellular resources and in some cases is lethal (Baltrus, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Maintenance of a mobile genetic element in host cells requires balancing the costs and benefits to the host or a sufficiently high transfer frequency.
source: Maintenance of a mobile genetic element in host cells requires balancing the costs and benefits to the host or a sufficiently high transfer frequency.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a general principle.

claim: Many mobile elements, especially ICEs, have been identified bioinformatically.
source: Many mobile elements, especially ICEs, have been identified bioinformatically (Bi et al., 2012; Guglielmini et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Many ICEs contain putative cargo genes.
source: Many of these ICEs contain putative cargo genes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an observation from bioinformatic analyses.

claim: The phenotypes conferred by putative cargo genes cannot be inferred from sequence.
source: However, the phenotypes conferred by these genes cannot be inferred from sequence nor are they easily detected experimentally (Cury et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: The phenotypes conferred by putative cargo genes are not easily detected experimentally.
source: However, the phenotypes conferred by these genes cannot be inferred from sequence nor are they easily detected experimentally (Cury et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: ICEBs1 is a relatively small (~20 kb) ICE found in most strains of Bacillus subtilis.
source: ICEBs1, a relatively small (~20 kb) ICE found in most strains of Bacillus subtilis, was identified bioinformatically (Burrus et al., 2002) and experimentally based on its regulation by cell-cell signaling (Auchtung et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: ICEBs1 was identified bioinformatically.
source: ICEBs1, a relatively small (~20 kb) ICE found in most strains of Bacillus subtilis, was identified bioinformatically (Burrus et al., 2002) and experimentally based on its regulation by cell-cell signaling (Auchtung et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: ICEBs1 was identified experimentally based on its regulation by cell-cell signaling.
source: ICEBs1, a relatively small (~20 kb) ICE found in most strains of Bacillus subtilis, was identified bioinformatically (Burrus et al., 2002) and experimentally based on its regulation by cell-cell signaling (Auchtung et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Most of the ICEBs1 genes needed for conjugation are grouped together in an operon that is repressed until activating signals are sensed.
source: Most of the ICEBs1 genes needed for conjugation are grouped together in an operon that is repressed until activating signals are sensed (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Two pathways activate ICEBs1, both of which lead to cleavage of the repressor ImmR by the protease and anti-repressor ImmA.
source: Two pathways activate ICEBs1, both of which lead to cleavage of the repressor ImmR by the protease and anti-repressor ImmA (Auchtung et al., 2007; Bose et al., 2008; Bose and Grossman, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: ICEBs1 contains the cell-cell signaling genes, rapI and phrI.
source: ICEBs1 contains the cell-cell signaling genes, rapI and phrI, which regulate ICEBs1 activation by sensing population density and the relative abundance of ICEBs1-containing host cells (Auchtung et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: rapI and phrI regulate ICEBs1 activation by sensing population density and the relative abundance of ICEBs1-containing host cells.
source: ICEBs1 contains the cell-cell signaling genes, rapI and phrI, which regulate ICEBs1 activation by sensing population density and the relative abundance of ICEBs1-containing host cells (Auchtung et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: RapI is produced at high cell density and during the transition to stationary phase.
source: RapI is produced at high cell density and during the transition to stationary phase and stimulates the proteolytic cleavage of the repressor ImmR by the protease ImmA (Bose and Grossman, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: RapI stimulates the proteolytic cleavage of the repressor ImmR by the protease ImmA.
source: RapI is produced at high cell density and during the transition to stationary phase and stimulates the proteolytic cleavage of the repressor ImmR by the protease ImmA (Bose and Grossman, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Overproduction of RapI stimulates activation of ICEBs1 in >90% of cells.
source: Overproduction of RapI stimulates activation of ICEBs1 in >90% of cells (Auchtung et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: RapI activity (and therefore ICEBs1 activation) is inhibited by PhrI.
source: RapI activity (and therefore ICEBs1 activation) is inhibited by PhrI, a peptide that is secreted by cells that contain ICEBs1.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a known regulatory mechanism.

claim: PhrI is a peptide that is secreted by cells that contain ICEBs1.
source: RapI activity (and therefore ICEBs1 activation) is inhibited by PhrI, a peptide that is secreted by cells that contain ICEBs1.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a known characteristic of PhrI.

claim: PhrI levels indicate the relative abundance of ICEBs1-containing cells in the population.
source: PhrI levels indicate the relative abundance of ICEBs1-containing cells in the population, preventing the activation and possible redundant transfer of ICEBs1 if most nearby cells already contain the element.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a known function of PhrI.

claim: PhrI prevents the activation and possible redundant transfer of ICEBs1 if most nearby cells already contain the element.
source: PhrI levels indicate the relative abundance of ICEBs1-containing cells in the population, preventing the activation and possible redundant transfer of ICEBs1 if most nearby cells already contain the element.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a known function of PhrI.

claim: ICEBs1 is also activated during the RecA-dependent DNA damage response.
source: ICEBs1 is also activated during the RecA-dependent DNA damage response (Auchtung et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Biofilms appear to be hotspots of horizontal gene transfer for bacteria growing in natural settings.
source: Biofilms appear to be hotspots of horizontal gene transfer for bacteria growing in natural settings (Madsen et al., 2012; Molin and Tolker-Nielsen, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Undomesticated strains of B. subtilis form complex biofilms on agar plates and at the air-liquid interface in standing cultures.
source: Undomesticated strains of B. subtilis form complex biofilms on agar plates and at the air-liquid interface in standing cultures (Vlamakis et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: There is extensive spore formation in B. subtilis biofilms.
source: There is also extensive spore formation in B. subtilis biofilms (Branda et al., 2001; Vlamakis et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: During growth in a biofilm, ICEBs1 is naturally activated and transfers efficiently, generating on the order of 10 new ICEBs1-containing host cells (transconjugants) per donor cell under appropriate conditions.
source: In addition, during growth in a biofilm, ICEBs1 is naturally activated and transfers efficiently, generating on the order of 10 new ICEBs1-containing host cells (transconjugants) per donor cell under appropriate conditions (Lécuyer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: B. subtilis biofilms are held together by a matrix composed of secreted exopolysaccharides, protein fibers, and DNA.
source: B. subtilis biofilms are held together by a matrix composed of secreted exopolysaccharides, protein fibers, and DNA (Vlamakis et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: The biofilm matrix reinforces cell-cell contacts, likely promoting rapid spread of ICEBs1 by conjugation.
source: This matrix reinforces cell-cell contacts, likely promoting rapid spread of ICEBs1 by conjugation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from the known properties of the biofilm matrix.

claim: The conditions that promote biofilm formation (high cell density) also promote activation and transfer of ICEBs1 and sporulation.
source: Additionally, the conditions that promote biofilm formation (high cell density) also promote activation and transfer of ICEBs1 and sporulation (Auchtung et al., 2005; Grossman and Losick, 1988).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: It is unknown how ICEBs1 impacts its host cells under biofilm growth conditions.
source: Although biofilm growth is clearly beneficial to conjugation, it is unknown how ICEBs1 impacts its host cells under these conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a knowledge gap.

claim: ICEBs1 spreads efficiently in biofilms by conjugation at low donor to recipient ratios.
source: We observed highly efficient spread of ICEBs1 at low donor to recipient ratios (Table 1) during growth in biofilms, similar to results reported previously (Lécuyer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Table 1 and a citation.

claim: After 4 days of biofilm growth, the frequency of transconjugants ranged from ~0.4 to 0.6 of total cells in the biofilm for starting donor frequencies of ~0.01–0.5.
source: We found that after four days of biofilm growth, the frequency of transconjugants ranged from ~0.4 to 0.6 of total cells in the biofilm for starting donor frequencies of ~0.01–0.5 (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Table 1.

claim: The highest frequency of transconjugants was observed when the starting frequency of ICEBs1-containing cells was ~0.1.
source: The highest frequency of transconjugants was observed when the starting frequency of ICEBs1-containing cells was ~0.1.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an observation from the mating experiments.

claim: Enhanced conjugation at low donor to recipient ratios is likely due to regulation of ICEBs1 by cell-cell signaling (induction is inhibited by the presence of other potential donors) and the higher likelihood of contacting potential recipients at low frequencies of donors.
source: Enhanced conjugation at low donor to recipient ratios is likely due to regulation of ICEBs1 by cell-cell signaling (induction is inhibited by the presence of other potential donors) and the higher likelihood of contacting potential recipients at low frequencies of donors.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the mating data.

claim: Cells containing ICEBs1 that is incapable of conjugation {ICEBs1(conEK476E)} had a fitness advantage over cells lacking ICEBs1 during biofilm growth when they were initially present as a minority of the population.
source: We found that cells containing ICEBs1 that is incapable of conjugation {ICEBs1(conEK476E)} had a fitness advantage over cells lacking ICEBs1 during biofilm growth when they were initially present as a minority of the population.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by competition experiment data.

claim: The fitness of ICEBs1-containing cells was dependent on their initial frequency in the population.
source: We found that the fitness of ICEBs1-containing cells was dependent on their initial frequency in the population (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 2A.

claim: Cells with ICEBs1 had a selective advantage at low frequencies (0.01 or 0.1) when the element is most strongly activated.
source: Cells with ICEBs1 had a selective advantage at low frequencies (0.01 or 0.1) when the element is most strongly activated.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by competition data.

claim: At high frequencies in the population (0.5 or 0.9), when there is little or no activation, fitness of ICEBs1-containing cells was approximately neutral.
source: At high frequencies in the population (0.5 or 0.9), when there is little or no activation, fitness of ICEBs1-containing cells was approximately neutral (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 2A.

claim: The final growth yields of the populations were similar regardless of the frequency of ICEBs1-containing cells.
source: The final growth yields of the populations were similar regardless of the frequency of ICEBs1-containing cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: The frequency-dependence of ICEBs1 fitness was most likely due to regulation of ICEBs1 gene expression by the cell-cell signaling genes rapI-phrI or some other function of rapI.
source: The frequency-dependence was most likely due to regulation of ICEBs1 gene expression by the cell-cell signaling genes rapI-phrI or some other function of rapI.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the frequency-dependent fitness data.

claim: In biofilms without sporulation, spo0A∆Ps mutant cells containing ICEBs1 had a selective advantage compared to spo0A∆Ps mutant cells without ICEBs1.
source: In biofilms without sporulation, spo0A∆Ps mutant cells containing ICEBs1 (JMJ788) had a selective advantage compared to spo0A∆Ps mutant cells without ICEBs1 (JMJ786) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 2E.

claim: Sporulation was not required for a fitness benefit to ICEBs1-containing cells in biofilms.
source: Thus, sporulation was not required for a fitness benefit to ICEBs1-containing cells in biofilms.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the spo0A∆Ps mutant experiments.

claim: Cells containing ICEBs1 'cheat' by decreasing expression of biofilm matrix genes compared to cells without ICEBs1.
source: We showed that cells containing ICEBs1 'cheat' by decreasing expression of biofilm matrix genes compared to cells without ICEBs1 (see below).
evidence: This is stated in the results and refers to data presented later in the manuscript.

claim: Cells containing ICEBs1 had a frequency-dependent selective advantage during sporulation, in the absence of biofilms.
source: We found that cells containing ICEBs1 also had a frequency-dependent selective advantage during sporulation, in the absence of biofilms.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by competition data on DSM agar.

claim: At an initial frequency of approximately 0.01 on DSM agar, the median relative fitness of the ICEBs1-containing cells was approximately 14.
source: At an initial frequency of approximately 0.01, the median relative fitness of the ICEBs1-containing cells was approximately 14 (14.5 ± 4.3).
evidence: This is stated in the results as a quantitative finding from competition experiments.

claim: Sporulation was required for the strong selective advantage during growth on sporulation medium (DSM agar).
source: We found that sporulation was required for the strong selective advantage during growth on sporulation medium (DSM agar).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by spo0A∆Ps mutant data.

claim: The fitness benefit associated with the ICEBs1-containing cells at a low frequency in the population was greatly reduced in the spo0A∆Ps mutant (no sporulation).
source: The fitness benefit associated with the ICEBs1-containing cells at a low frequency in the population was greatly reduced in the spo0A∆Ps mutant (no sporulation) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 2F.

claim: The sporulation mutant with ICEBs1 had a median fitness of approximately 1.5 compared to approximately nine for wild-type.
source: The sporulation mutant with ICEBs1 had a median fitness of approximately 1.5 compared to approximately nine for wild-type.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a quantitative comparison.

claim: Cells containing ICEBs1 have a frequency-dependent selective advantage in biofilms and during sporulation.
source: Together, our results demonstrate that cells containing ICEBs1 have a frequency-dependent selective advantage in biofilms and during sporulation.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a summary of the competition experiments.

claim: This selective advantage is independent of the ability of ICEBs1 to actually transfer from one cell to another.
source: This selective advantage is independent of the ability of ICEBs1 to actually transfer from one cell to another.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from experiments using the conEK476E mutation.

claim: Biofilm formation and sporulation are both regulated by the transcription factor Spo0A.
source: Biofilm formation (Hamon and Lazazzera, 2001) and sporulation (Hoch, 1993; Sonenshein, 2000) are both regulated by the transcription factor Spo0A.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations.

claim: The presence of ICEBs1 could somehow be inhibiting the activity or activation of Spo0A.
source: Our results indicate that the presence of ICEBs1 could somehow be inhibiting the activity or activation of Spo0A.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the fitness and developmental data.

claim: In mixed populations, sporulation was delayed in cells containing ICEBs1 compared to cells without ICEBs1, in a frequency-dependent manner.
source: We found that in mixed populations, sporulation was delayed in cells containing ICEBs1 compared to cells without ICEBs1, in a frequency-dependent manner.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by time-course data.

claim: When ICEBs1-containing cells were started at a frequency of approximately 0.01 in biofilms, they reached their maximum sporulation frequency (>80% spores) roughly 17 hr later than the cells without ICEBs1.
source: When ICEBs1-containing cells were started at a frequency of approximately 0.01, they reached their maximum sporulation frequency (>80% spores) roughly 17 hr later than the cells without ICEBs1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3A.

claim: After 3 days of biofilm growth, the sporulation frequencies of ICEBs1-containing and ICEBs1-cured cells were indistinguishable.
source: After 3 days of biofilm growth, the sporulation frequencies of ICEBs1-containing and ICEBs1-cured cells were indistinguishable.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an observation from time-course experiments.

claim: When the ICEBs1-containing cells were the majority in the population (initial frequency ~0.9) the timing and sporulation frequencies of the ICEBs1-containing and ICEBs1-cured cells were indistinguishable.
source: When the ICEBs1-containing cells were the majority in the population (initial frequency ~0.9) the timing and sporulation frequencies of the ICEBs1-containing and ICEBs1-cured cells were indistinguishable (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: Sporulation of ICEBs1-containing cells was delayed in a frequency-dependent manner during sporulation in the absence of biofilm formation.
source: We also found that sporulation of ICEBs1-containing cells was delayed in a frequency-dependent manner during sporulation in the absence of biofilm formation (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: The stronger selective advantage of ICEBs1-containing cells on sporulation medium is due to the earlier onset of sporulation.
source: We suspect that the stronger selective advantage of ICEBs1-containing cells on sporulation medium is due to the earlier onset of sporulation.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the fitness differences between biofilm and sporulation conditions.

claim: By 16 hr of growth on sporulation medium, spores made up about 40% of the total CFUs.
source: By 16 hr of growth on sporulation medium, spores made up about 40% of the total CFUs.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a quantitative observation.

claim: By 16 hr in biofilms, spores were undetectable (limit of detection ~0.03% spores).
source: By the same time in biofilms, spores were undetectable (limit of detection ~0.03% spores).
evidence: This is stated in the results as a quantitative observation.

claim: The fitness benefits provided by ICEBs1 were dependent on the relative abundance of ICEBs1-containing cells.
source: The fitness benefits provided by ICEBs1 were dependent on the relative abundance of ICEBs1-containing cells, indicating that the cell-cell signaling genes rapI-phrI in ICEBs1 were likely involved, either directly or indirectly.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the frequency-dependent fitness data.

claim: The cell-cell signaling genes rapI-phrI in ICEBs1 were likely involved in the fitness benefits, either directly or indirectly.
source: The fitness benefits provided by ICEBs1 were dependent on the relative abundance of ICEBs1-containing cells, indicating that the cell-cell signaling genes rapI-phrI in ICEBs1 were likely involved, either directly or indirectly.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the frequency-dependent fitness data.

claim: Other Rap proteins in B. subtilis are known to regulate development by inhibiting phosphorylation (activation) of the transcription factor Spo0A.
source: Other Rap proteins in B. subtilis are known to regulate development by inhibiting phosphorylation (activation) of the transcription factor Spo0A (Sonenshein, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by a citation.

claim: RapI, like other Rap proteins in B. subtilis, can inhibit the pathway needed to phosphorylate (activate) the transcription factor Spo0A.
source: RapI, like other Rap proteins in B. subtilis, can inhibit the pathway needed to phosphorylate (activate) the transcription factor Spo0A, and overexpression of rapI in vivo inhibits sporulation (Even-Tov et al., 2016; Parashar et al., 2013; Singh et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations.

claim: Overexpression of rapI in vivo inhibits sporulation.
source: RapI, like other Rap proteins in B. subtilis, can inhibit the pathway needed to phosphorylate (activate) the transcription factor Spo0A, and overexpression of rapI in vivo inhibits sporulation (Even-Tov et al., 2016; Parashar et al., 2013; Singh et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations.

claim: It was unknown whether RapI regulates development in vivo under physiological conditions.
source: However, it was unknown whether RapI regulates development in vivo under physiological conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a knowledge gap.

claim: The rapI-phrI system is required for the fitness advantage of ICEBs1-containing cells.
source: Results described below demonstrate that the rapI-phrI system is required for the fitness advantage of ICEBs1-containing cells, but that this requirement is by virtue of causing induction of ICEBs1 gene expression.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by deletion mutant data.

claim: The requirement for rapI-phrI is by virtue of causing induction of ICEBs1 gene expression.
source: Results described below demonstrate that the rapI-phrI system is required for the fitness advantage of ICEBs1-containing cells, but that this requirement is by virtue of causing induction of ICEBs1 gene expression.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from genetic experiments.

claim: Another gene in ICEBs1 is both necessary and sufficient for the selective advantage of ICEBs1-containing cells during development.
source: Another gene in ICEBs1 is both necessary and sufficient for the selective advantage of ICEBs1-containing cells during development.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a preview of findings about devI.

claim: Locked-in ICEBs1 still conferred a fitness benefit to host cells.
source: We verified that locked-in ICEBs1 still conferred a fitness benefit to host cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by competition data.

claim: During sporulation in biofilms (MSgg agar), cells containing locked-in ICEBs1 had a relative fitness of approximately 14 when they were started at a low frequency in the population (~0.01).
source: During sporulation in biofilms (MSgg agar), cells containing locked-in ICEBs1 had a relative fitness of approximately 14 when they were started at a low frequency in the population (~0.01) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 4A.

claim: The benefit of locked-in ICEBs1 was much greater than that conferred by wild-type ICEBs1 that can excise and replicate.
source: This benefit was much greater than that conferred by wild-type ICEBs1 that can excise and replicate.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a comparison between locked-in and wild-type ICEBs1.

claim: Replication of ICEBs1 incurs a fitness cost to the host cell that reduces the apparent benefit.
source: We suspect that replication of ICEBs1 incurs a fitness cost to the host cell that reduces the apparent benefit.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the fitness difference between locked-in and wild-type ICEBs1.

claim: rapI-phrI were required for the fitness benefit conferred by ICEBs1.
source: We found that rapI-phrI were required for the fitness benefit conferred by ICEBs1.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by deletion mutant data.

claim: During sporulation in biofilms (MSgg agar), the relative fitness of the ∆(rapI-phrI) host strain was approximately neutral.
source: During sporulation in biofilms (MSgg agar), the relative fitness of the ∆(rapI-phrI) host strain was approximately neutral (Figure 4A), in contrast to the high fitness (median ~14) provided by ICEBs1 containing rapI-phrI when the ICEBs1-containing cells were started at a low frequency (~0.01).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 4A.

claim: rapI-phrI alone were not sufficient to provide a fitness benefit during sporulation or during sporulation in biofilms.
source: We found that rapI-phrI alone were not sufficient to provide a fitness benefit during sporulation or during sporulation in biofilms.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ectopic expression data.

claim: When a strain with ectopic rapI-phrI was started at a low frequency (~0.01), fitness of this strain was neutral relative to a control strain without rapI-phrI.
source: When this strain was started at a low frequency (~0.01), fitness of this strain was neutral relative to a control strain without rapI-phrI (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: Adding the rest of ICEBs1 to ectopic rapI-phrI restored the fitness advantage during sporulation and in biofilms.
source: To verify that rapI-phrI were functional, we added back ICEBs1 that was missing rapI-phrI. Adding the rest of ICEBs1 restored the fitness advantage during sporulation and in biofilms, indicating that the ectopic copy of rapI-phrI was functional (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 4B.
